NOTE 66

In this note we prove that form 322 $(KW(WO,\,\infty ))$ is true in $\mathcal{N}1$. (Brunner [1982a], (Proposition 4.5) also has a proof of this result.)

Assume that $X$ is a well ordered set in $\mathcal{N}1$ and that $\forall y\in X,\,|y|\geq 2$. Let $E$ be a (finite) support of a well ordering of $X$ and let fix$(E)$ be the group of permutations of $A$ (the set of atoms) which fix $E$ pointwise. Then for all $\phi \in$ fix$(E)$, $\phi$ fixes $X$ pointwise. Choose an atom $a\in A-E$. We will show that for every $y\in X,\,E\cup \{a\}$ is a support of a non-empty proper subset $y^{\prime }$ of $y$. This will suffice since it follows that the function $y\mapsto y^{\prime }$ is in $\mathcal{N}1$.

Choose an element $y\in X$. If every element of $y$ has support $E$ then any nonempty proper subset of $y$ has support $E$ and therefore has support $E\cup \{a\}$. So we may assume that $y$ has some element $t$ such that $E$ is not a support of $t$. Choose a finite non-empty subset $F$ of $A$ such that $E\cap F=\emptyset$ and $E\cup F$ is a support of $t$ and such that $F$ is minimal in the sense that for no proper subset $F^{\prime }$ of $F$ is $E\cup F^{\prime }$ a support of $t$. We may assume without loss of generality that $a\in F$. (If $a\not \in F$ then we replace $t$ by $\psi (t)$ and $F$ by $\psi (F)$ where $\psi$ is a permutation of $A$ chosen so that $\psi \in$ fix$(E)$ and $a\in \psi (F).)$ Let $y'=\{\phi (t):\phi \in$ fix$(E\cup \{a\})\}$. Clearly $y^{\prime }$ has support $E\cup \{a\},\,y^{\prime }\subseteq y$ and $y^{\prime }\neq \emptyset$ (since $t\in y^{\prime }$). It only remains to show that $y^{\prime }\neq y$.

Choose an $\eta \in$ fix$(E)$ so that $\eta (F) \cap F=\emptyset$. Then for every $\phi \in$ fix$(E\cup \{a\})$, $\eta (F)\neq \phi (F)$. It follows from the lemma that for all such $\phi ,\,\eta (t)\neq \phi (t)$. Therefore $\eta (t)\in (y-y^{\prime })$.

NOTE 70

We give a proof that form [62 E] $(KW(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}))$ implies form 62 $(C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}))$. Let $x$ be a set of finite sets and let $y=\{u:(\exists v\in x)u\subseteq v\}$. By [62 E], there is a Kinna-Wagner selection function, $f$, on $y$. We define a choice function $g$ on $x$ as follows: Let $u\in x$ be such that $|u|=n$. There exists an $m\in \omega ,\,m<n$, such that $f^{m}(u)$ is a singleton. Define $g(u)$ to be the single element of $f^{m}(u)$. (Form 323, $KW(WO,\,\infty )$, clearly implies [62 E].)

NOTE 71

In this note we give definitions from Morillon [1988] for forms [14 L], [14 BP] through [14 BX], [14 CC] through [14 CH], [118 I] through [118 T], 331, 332, 343, 344, and [345 C] through [345 E].

Let $X$ be a topological space, let $E=\{(A,\,B):A$ and $B$ are closed in $X$ and $A \cap B=\emptyset \}$ and let $F=\{(U,\,V):U$ and $V$ are open in $X$ and $U\cap V=\emptyset$}.

1.

$f:E\rightarrow F$ is a normality operator on $X$ if $\forall (A,\,B)\in E,\,f(A,\, B)=(U,\,V)$ where $A\subseteq U$ and $B\subseteq V$.

2.

$X$ is effectively normal if $X$ is $T_{2}$ and there is a normality operator on $X$.

3.

$X$ is hereditarily normal (or completely normal) if all subspaces of $X$ are normal.

4.

$X$ is hereditarily effectively normal if all subspaces of $X$ are effectively normal.

5.

A set $I\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ is discrete if $\forall x\in X,\,\exists$ a neighborhood $N$ of $x$ such that $N\cap A\neq \emptyset$ for at most one element $A\in I$.

6.

$X$ is collectionwise normal if $X$ is $T_{2}$ and for every discrete $I\subseteq \{U:U$ is closed in $S\}$ there is a set $J$ of pairwise disjoint open subsets of $X$ such that for every $F\in I,\,\exists U\in J$ such that $F\subseteq U$.

7.

Let $D=${ $I:I$ is a discrete collection of closed subsets of $X$} and $O=\{J:J$ is a collection of pairwise disjoint open subsets of $X$}. Then $f:D\rightarrow O$ is a collectionwise normality operator on $X$ if $\forall I\in D$, if $f(I)=J$ then $\forall F\in I,\,\exists U\in J$ such that $F\subseteq U$. $N_{c}(X)$ denotes the set of collectionwise normality operators on $X$.

8.

$X$ is effectively collectionwise normal if X is $T_{2}$ and $N_{c}(X)\neq \emptyset$.

9.

$X$ is highly separated if $X$ is $T_{2}$ and $\{N_{c}(F):F\subseteq X\}$ has a choice function.

10.

$X$ is functionally separated if for all pairs $(A,\,B)$ of closed disjoint subsets of $X$ there is a function $f:X\rightarrow [0,\,1]$ such that $A\subseteq f^{-1}(0)$ and $B\subseteq f^{-1}(1)$.

11.

$X$ is Tietze-Urysohn if for every closed $F\subseteq X$ and every continuous function $f:F\rightarrow [0,\,1]$ there is a continuous function $g:X\rightarrow [0,\,1]$ which extends $f$.

12.

Let $C=${ $g:g:X\rightarrow [0, 1]$ and $g$ is continuous}. A function $f:E\rightarrow C$ is a Urysohn operator on $X$ if $\forall (A,\,B)\in E$, if $U=f(A,\,B)$ then $A\subseteq U^{-1}(0)$ and $B\subseteq U^{-1}(1)$. $U(X)$ denotes the set of Urysohn operators on $X$.

13.

Let $B=\{(F,\,U):F$ is a closed subset of $X$ and $U:F\rightarrow [0, 1]$ is continuous}. A function $f:B\rightarrow C$ is a Tietze-Urysohn operator if $\forall (F,\,U)\in B$, if $f(F,\, U)=V$ then $V$ extends $U$.

14.

$X$ is effectively functionally separated if $U(X)\neq \emptyset$. $X$ is effectively Tietze-Urysohn if T-U$(X$) $\neq \emptyset$. (Where T-U($X$) is the set of all Tietze-Urysohn operators on $X$.)

15.

$X$ is highly functionally separated if $\{U(A):A\subseteq X\}$ has a choice function.

16.

$X$ is highly Tietze-Urysohn if {T-U$(A):A\subseteq X\}$ has a choice function.

17.

$X$ is collectionwise separated (or collectionwise Hausdorff) if it is $T_{2}$ and for every discrete set $I$ of singletons from $X$ there is a set $J$ of open subsets of $X$ such that for every $F\in I$, there is a unique $O\in J$ containing (the singleton) $F$.

Assume that $(X,\,\leq )$ is a linear order.

18.

$A\subseteq X$ is convex if $\forall (x,\,y)\in A^{2},\,\forall u\in X$, if $x<u<y$ then $u\in A$.

19.

$(X, \leq )$ is conditionally complete if each non-empty subset with an upper bound has a least upper bound and each non-empty subset with a lower bound has a greatest lower bound.

20.

$(X,\,\leq )$ is complete if $X=\emptyset$ or every subset has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound.

21.

Let $X$ be a topological space, let $E$ be defined as above and let $\Omega (X)$ be the set of open subsets of $X$. A function $f:E\rightarrow \Omega (X)$ is a monotone normality operator on $X$ if for every $(F,\,G)\in E$ the following conditions hold

(i)

$F\subseteq f(F,\,G)\subseteq \overline{f(F,\,G)}\subseteq X-G$.

(ii)

If $(F^{\prime },\,G^{\prime })\in E,\,F\subseteq F^{\prime }$ and $G^{\prime }\subseteq G$ then $f(F,\,G)\subseteq f(F^{\prime },\,G^{\prime })$.

22.

A topological space $X$ is monotonely normal if it is $T_{1}$ and there is a monotone normality operator on $X$.

23.

Let $(X,\,\leq )$ be a complete linear order and let $E$ be the set of non-empty open intervals of $X$. An increasing choice function on $(X,\,\leq )$ is a function $\ast :E\rightarrow X$ such that

(i)

$\forall I\in E,\,\ast (I)\in I$.

(ii)

If $(a,\,b)\in E$ and $(b,\,c)\in E$ then $\ast ((a,\,b))\leq \ast ((a,\,c))\leq \ast ((b,\,c))$.

24.

A topological space $X$ is completely regular if for all open $U\subseteq X$ and all $p\in U$, there is a continuous $f:X\rightarrow [0,\,1]$ such that $f(p)=0$ and $\forall x\in X-U,\,f(x)=1$.

25.

An ordered set $(T,\,\leq )$ is a lattice if any two elements have a greatest lower bound and a least upper bound. A lattice is bounded is it has a smallest and largest element.

26.

An ideal $I$ in a lattice $(T,\,\leq )$ is prime if $\forall x,\,y\in T$, if $x\wedge y\in I$ then either $x\in I$ or $y\in I$.

27.

If $T$ is a bounded distributive lattice a function $f$ is a prime ideal choice function on $T$ if for each proper ideal $I$ of $T,\,f(I)$ is a prime ideal containing $I$.

28.

Assume that $T$ is a bounded distributive lattice in which every subset has a least upper bound then $T$ is $\vee$-compact if for all $F\subseteq T$ such that $\bigvee F=1$, there is a finite $F^{\prime }\subseteq F$ such that $\bigvee F^{\prime }=1.$ (If $(\Omega ,\,\subseteq )$ is the lattice of open sets of a topological space $X$ then $X$ is compact if and only if $(\Omega ,\,\subseteq )$ is $\vee$-compact.)

29.

Let $E$ be a set. An ultra filter choice function $f$ on $E$ is a function such that for all proper filters $I$ in $\mathcal{P}(E)$, $f(I)$ is an ultra filter containing $I$.

30.

Let $E$ be a set and $U$ an ultra filter on a set $I$. $U$ is $E$-adequate if for every filter $F$ in $\mathcal{P}(E)$ there is a function $g:I\rightarrow E$ such that $g(U)$ contains $F$.

31.

A topological space is irreducible if it is not empty and is not the union of two proper closed subsets.

32.

A topological space $X$ is sober if every closed irreducible subset of $X$ is the closure of a unique singleton.

33.

A Banach algebra is a normed algebra in which every Cauchy filter converges.

34.

Let $(I,\,\leq )$ be a preorder (reflexive and transitive), let $(E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I}$ be a family of sets and for each $(\alpha ,\,\beta )\in I\times I$ let $f_{\alpha ,\beta }$ be a function from $E_{\beta }$ to $E_{\alpha }$. Assume that the $f_{\alpha ,\beta }$ satisfy the following conditions:

$(LP_{I})\ \alpha \leq \beta \leq \gamma \Rightarrow f_{\alpha ,\gamma }=f_{\alpha ,\beta }\circ f_{\beta ,\gamma }$.

$(LP_{II})$ For all $\alpha \in I,\,f_{\alpha ,\alpha }$ is the identity on $E_{\alpha }$.

Then $((E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I})$ is called a projective system relative to the preorder $(I,\,\leq )$. Let $E=\prod _{\alpha \in I}E_{\alpha }$ and for each pair $(\alpha ,\,\beta )\in I\times I$ such that $\alpha \leq \beta$, let $E_{\alpha ,\beta }=\{x\in E:f_{\alpha ,\beta }(x_{\beta })=x_{\alpha }\}$. Then the set $Y=\bigcap _{\alpha <\beta }E_{\alpha ,\beta }$ is called the projective limit of the projective system $((E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I})$. $Y$ is denoted $\lim _{\leftarrow }(E_{\alpha },\,f_{\alpha ,\beta })$. In case the preorder $(I,\,\leq )$ is directed to the right (that is, $\forall (\alpha ,\,\beta )\in I^{2},\,\exists \gamma \in I$ such that $\alpha \leq \gamma$ and $\beta \leq \gamma$.) we say that the projective system $((E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\, (f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I})$ is directed.

35.

If $((X_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I})$ is a projective system relative to the preorder $(I, \leq )$ and if each $X_{\alpha }$ has a topology $C_{\alpha }$ such that $f_{\alpha ,\beta }$ is continuous relative to the topologies $C_{\alpha }$ and $C_{\beta }$ then the system $((X_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I})$ is called $a$ projective system of topological spaces. In this case the projective limit of the system with the topology induced by the product topology on $\prod _{\alpha \in I}X_{\alpha }$ is called the the projective limit of the projective system of topological spaces.

36.

If $(A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee )$ is a bounded, distributive lattice, $X$ is a subset of $A$ and $F$ is a filter in $A$, then $F$ respects $X$ if $X\subseteq F$ and $\bigwedge X$ exists implies $\bigwedge X\in F$.

37.

If $(A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee )$ is a bounded, distributive lattice, $X$ is a subset of $A$ and $F$ is a filter in $A$, then $F$ strongly respects $X$ if $X\subseteq F$ implies $\exists y\in F$ such that $\forall x\in X,\,y\leq x$.

38.

If $X$ is a subset of a bounded, distributive lattice $(A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee )$ then $X$ is of Boolean type if for all $b\in A,\,[(\forall x\in X,\,b\vee x=1)$ and $(\forall y\leq X,\,y\leq b)]$ implies $b=1$. $(y\leq X$ means $(\forall x\in X)(y\leq x).)$

39.

If $(A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee )$ is a bounded, distributive lattice we say that A has the Rasiowa-Sikorski property (respectively the strong Rasiowa-Sikorski property) if for all $a,\,b\in A$ such that $a\not \leq b$ and all sequences $(X_{n})_{n\in \omega }$ of subsets of $A$ of Boolean type there is a prime filter containing $a$, not containing $b$ and respecting (respectively strongly respecting) each $X_{n}$.

40.

If $(A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee )$ is a bounded distributive lattice then an element $a\in A$ is $\vee$-compact if for every subset $I\subseteq A,\,\bigvee I=a$ implies $(\exists J\subseteq I)$ ($J$ finite and $\bigvee J=a$).

NOTE 72

We prove that form $207(\beta )$ implies 209 for any ordinal $\beta$. (form $207(\beta )$ is $UT(\aleph _{\beta },\,\aleph _{\beta },\,<2^{\aleph _{\beta }})$ and 209 is ($\exists$ an ordinal $\alpha$) $(\forall X)$ (If $X$ is a denumerable union of denumerable sets then $\mathcal{P}(X)$ cannot be partitioned into $\aleph _{\alpha }$ non-empty sets.)) Assume form $207(\beta )$ is true. Then for any set $X$, if $X$ is a denumerable union of denumerable sets, then $|X|<2^{\aleph _{\beta }}$. Choose an ordinal $\alpha$ so that $\neg (\aleph _{\alpha }\leq |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(2^{\aleph _{\beta }}))|)$. For any $X$ which is the denumerable union of denumerable sets we have $|\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(X))|\leq |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(2^{\aleph _{\beta }}))|$. A partition of $\mathcal{P}(X)$ into $\aleph _{\alpha }$ non-empty sets would give $\aleph _{\alpha }\leq |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(X))|$.

Similarly, form 26 implies form 209 and form 31 implies form 209.

Model A ($\mathcal{M}43$). Form 62 $(C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}))$ and form 43 (DC) are true and form 30 (OP) is false.

Model B ($\mathcal{M}44$). Forms 30 and 43 are true and form 15 (Kinna-Wagner Principle) is false.

Model C $(\mathcal{M}45)$. Forms 30 and 43 are true and form 49 (the order extension principle) is false.

Model D $(\mathcal{M}46(n,\,M))$. For each finite set $Z$ of positive natural numbers and natural number $n>1$, for which the following is false

$S(Z,\,n)$: For every decomposition $n=p_{1}+\ldots +p_{s}$ of $n$ into a sum of primes at least one $p_{i}$ divides and element of $Z$, (See Mostowski [1945]. Also see note 15. Condition $S$ implies condition $D$ of note 15.)

there is a model in which form 46 $(C(\infty ,\,Z))$ and form 43 are true and form 45 $(C(\infty ,\,n))$ is false.

Model E $(\mathcal{M}47(n,\,M))$. For every finite set $Z$ of positive integers and integer $n>1$, for which the following condition is false

$M(Z,\,n)$: For any decomposition $n=p_{1}+\ldots +p_{s}$ of $n$ into a sum of primes there are non-negative $q_{1},\,\ldots$, $q_{s}$ such that $q_{1}p_{1}+\ldots +q_{s}p_{s}\in Z$.

There is a model in which form 46 $(C(\infty ,\,Z))$ and form 43 are true and form 47 $(C(WO,\,n))$ is false. (See Mostowski [1945]. Also, condition $K$ of note 15 implies condition $M$.)

NOTE 75

Several weak forms of AC are known to be equivalent to AC in ZF. These include:

1.

MC: The Axiom of Multiple Choice, form 67;

2.

LW: Every linearly ordered set can be well ordered, form 90;

3.

PW: The power set of a well ordered set can be well ordered, form 91;

4.

VB: Every vector space has a basis, form 66;

5.

A: The Antichain Principle, form 89; and

6.

$C(LO,\,\infty )$: Every linearly ordered family of non-empty sets has a choice function, form 202.

Consequently everything that implies one of these six forms is equivalent to AC in ZF. That is, 95, 109, 112, 114, 133, 147, 149, 164, 218, 264, 292, 333, 334, and $335(n)$ for $n\geq 2$, also imply AC in ZF. In fact in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ the following two chains of implications are provable: AC $\rightarrow$ VB $\rightarrow$ MC $\rightarrow$ A $\rightarrow$ LW $\rightarrow$ PW, and AC $\rightarrow C(LO,\,\infty )\rightarrow$ LW. With regard to the reverse implications, VB $\rightarrow$ AC, MC $\rightarrow$ VB and LW $\rightarrow C(LO,\,\infty )$ are open questions. The other reverse implications are known to be unprovable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. (See Jech [1973b], page 134, Felgner/Jech [1973], Blass [1984a], H. Rubin [1960], H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985], Part I, 5, Brunner [1983a],[1984b],[1985a], Howard/Rubin [1977], Truss [1978], Keremedis [1996a],[1996], and note 18.) It follows from the two chains of implications that each of the twenty forms mentioned above implies PW, form 91, in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$.

In Pincus [1972], page 740, it is shown that if $\neg \Phi$ is boundable (see Pincus [1972], p. 722 for the definition of boundable) and $\Phi \rightarrow AC$ is a theorem of ZF, then $\Phi \rightarrow$ form 91 (PW) is a theorem of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$.

NOTE 76

In this note we prove that form 126 $(MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ))$ implies forms 82 (If a set is infinite then its power set is Dedekind infinite.) and 185 (Every Dedekind finite, linearly ordered set is finite.)

It is clear from the lemma that $MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )$ implies that the power set of an infinite set is Dedekind infinite. To show that $MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )$ implies form 185, let $X$ be a Dedekind finite set which is linearly ordered by $\leq$. The assumption that $X$ is infinite leads to a contradiction as follows: By the lemma we get a sequence $(Y_{n})_{n\in \omega }$ of finite subsets of $X$ such that $Y_{n}\subsetneq Y_{n+1}$ for all $n\in \omega$. If we define $t_{n}$ to be the $\leq$-least element of $Y_{n+1}-Y_{n}$ then $(t_{n})_{n\in \omega }$ is an infinite sequence of distinct elements of $X$ and therefore $X$ is Dedekind infinite.

NOTE 81

We argue that form 30 (the ordering principle) implies form 83 (If every subset of $\mathcal{P}(X)$ which is linearly ordered by $\subseteq$ has a maximum element then $X$ is finite.)

Assume $X$ is infinite and let $\leq$ be a linear ordering of $X$. There must be either a non-empty subset $Y$ of $X$ with no least element (under $\leq$) or a non-empty subset with no greatest element. (If every non-empty subset of $X$ has a least element then let $x_{1}$ be the least element of $X,\,x_{2}$ be the least element of $X-\{x_{1}\}$, etc. This produces a subset $\{x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\ldots \}$ with no greatest element.) If $Y$ is an infinite subset of $X$ with no greatest element, we get a linearly ordered subset $A$ of $\mathcal{P}(X)$ with no maximum by letting $A=\{\{x:x\in Y\wedge x\leq y\}:y\in Y\}$. We can proceed similarly if $Y$ is an infinite subset of $X$ with no smallest element.

NOTE 88

Either $\mathcal{N}1$ or $\mathcal{N}3$ may be used to prove that form 31 $(UT(\aleph ^{0},\,\aleph ^{0},\,\aleph ^{0}))$ does not imply form 9 (Dedekind finite $=$ finite). Form 9 is known to be false in these models and a proof that form 31 holds is given below. The result is transferable to ZF by Pincus [1972].

Let $\mathcal{N}$ be either $\mathcal{N}1$ or $\mathcal{N}3$ with set of atoms $A$ and $\mathcal{G}$ the group of permutations used in defining the model. Assume that in $\mathcal{N},\,B$ is a denumerable set of denumerable sets. Let $e\subseteq A$ be a finite support for every $b\in B$. Such an $e$ exists since $B$ is well orderable in $\mathcal{N}$. Assume $b\in B$ and $x\in b$. The proof will be completed by showing that $e$ is a support of $x$. We argue by contradiction. Assume that $e$ is not a support of $x$. We will show that under this assumption $b$ has a subset of the same cardinality as an infinite subset of $A$ which contradicts the countability of $b$.

Let $e^{\prime }\supseteq e$ be a support of $x$. Then there is a $t\in e^{\prime }\backslash e$ and a $\phi \in \mathcal{G}$ which fixes $e^{\prime }\backslash \{t\}$ pointwise and such that $\phi (x)\neq x$. (It follows that $\phi (t)\neq t$.) It can be verified that

$$\begin{equation*} \{\langle \psi (t),\psi (x)\rangle :\psi \in \mathcal{G}\ {\text{and}}\ \psi \ {\text{fixes}}\ e^{\prime }\backslash \{t\}\ {\text{pointwise}}\} \end{equation*}$$

is a one to one function from an infinite subset of $A$ into $b$ which is in $\mathcal{N}$.

NOTE 91

In this note we argue that form 269 is false in the first Fraenkel model $\mathcal{N}1$ of ZF$^{0}$. Form 269 is: “For every cardinal $m$, there is a set $A$ such that $2^{|A|^{2}}\geq m$ and there is a choice function on the collection of 2 element subsets of $A$.” It suffices to show that for any set $A$ in $\mathcal{N}1$ if the set $[A]^{2}$ of two element subset of $A$ has a choice function, then $A$ is well orderable in $\mathcal{N}1$. Assume that $A$ is such a set and assume that $E$ is a (finite) support of $A$ and a choice function $f$ on $[A]^{2}$. Assume $x\in A$. We show by contradiction that $E$ must be a support of $x$. Suppose not and let $F$ be a support of $x$ containing $E$. We claim there is a permutation $\psi$ in $\mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)$ and an element $y\in A$ such that $x\neq y,\,\psi (x)=y$ and $\psi (y)=x$. This would contradict our choice of $E$ as a support for a choice function on $[A]^{2}$ since $\psi$ fixes $\{x,\,y\}$ but moves both of its elements. To get such a $\psi$, let $\phi \in \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)$ satisfy $\phi (x)\neq x$ and $\phi$ moves only finitely many atoms. Assume $F-E=\{t_{1},\,\ldots ,\,t_{n}\}$ and choose a set of atoms $\{s_{1},\,\ldots ,\, s_{n}\}$ disjoint from $F\cup \{t\in U:\phi (t)\neq t\}$. Let $\psi$ be the product of transpositions $\prod _{i=1}^{n}(t_{i},\,s_{i})$. The element $\psi (x)$ is different from $x$ since $\phi (x)\neq x$ and $\phi (\psi (x))=\psi (x)$. It is also clear that if $y=\psi (x)$, then $\psi (y)=x$.

NOTE 92

In Kolany/Wojtylak [1991] some relationships between forms 271$(m)$ and 45$(n)$ are given. $(271(n)$ is $CT_{n}$: The for the propositional calculus restricted to sets of formulas where each variable occurs in at most $n$ formulas, and $45(n)$ is $C(\infty ,\,n).)$ For example, $CT_{m}$ implies $C(\infty ,\,n)$ if $m\geq n!+n(n-1)$. Also considered are forms $CT_{m}^{\ast }\ (CT_{m}$ restricted to formulas which are disjunctions of formulas of the form $p$ or $(\neg p)$ where $p$ is a propositional variable). For example, it is shown that $CT_{3}^{\ast }$ implies $C(\infty ,\,2)$.

In this note we summarize what is known about the relationships between possible definitions of “finite”.

Several authors have studied this topic they include Diel [1974], Howard/Yorke [1989], Levy [1958], Spis̆iak [1993], Spis̆iak/Vojtás̆ [1988], Tarski [1938b] and [1954a], Truss [1974a] and Hickman [1972a]. The first eight definitions and their names are due to Tarski [1954a]

In Howard/Yorke [1989] the following definition is introduced:

It is shown there that IV $\rightarrow D$ and $D\rightarrow$ VII. Further, $V \not \rightarrow D$ and $D\not \rightarrow$ VI.

In Truss [1974a] the following classes of Dedekind finite cardinals are considered:

It is shown that each of $\mathrm{I}^{\prime \prime }, \mathrm{Ia}^{\prime \prime }, \mathrm{II}^{\prime \prime }$ and $\mathrm{III}^{\prime \prime }$ are equivalent to I and that the following implications hold: III $\rightarrow \mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime }\rightarrow \mathrm{IV},\mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime }\rightarrow \mathrm{VI}^{\prime \prime } \rightarrow \mathrm{V}$, and $\mathrm{VII}\rightarrow \mathrm{VI}^{\prime \prime }$. Further it is consistent (with $\mathrm{ZF}$) that there exists a set with any combination of the properties $\mathrm{III},\mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime },\mathrm{VI}^{\prime \prime }, \mathrm{IV}$ and $\mathrm{V}$ not excluded by the known implications described so far in this note. Finally, it is shown that form 88 $(C(\infty ,\,2))$ implies that $\mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime }$ and III are equivalent.

In addition, in Howard/Yorke [1989], if $J$ and $K$ are two possible definitions of finite then the assertion that $J$ and $K$ are equivalent is denoted by $E(J,\,K)$ and the strength of these weak forms of $AC$ is investigated. Several of these appear in the list of forms: $E(I,\,IV)$ is form 9, $E(I,\,Ia)$ is form 64, $E(I,\,III)$ is form 82, $E(I,\,II)$ is form 83, $E(II,\,III)$ is form 84, $E(II,\,IV)$ is form [9 B], $E(IV,\,V)$ is form [3 E], $E(V,\,VI)$ is form [1 AH], $E(VI,\,VII)$ is form [1 AI], $E(V^{\prime \prime },\,III)$ is form 276 and $E(D,\,VII)$ is form 277.

We note that $E(I,\,D)$ which is equivalent to “every infinite set is decomposable” is equivalent to the axiom of choice since it is form CN 4F in H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985], p. 139.

NOTE 95

Form [154 A] appears in Brunner [1984b] as $T_{\omega }$ and there Brunner refers to Brunner [1983b] for the result that form [154 A] is not provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. In Brunner [1983b] (p 437 Satz 2.2 (5)), the result $(tych_{2}(\omega )$ + form 106) $\Leftrightarrow DC$ appears, that is,

$$\begin{equation*} (\mathrm{form}\ 154 + \mathrm{form}\ 106)\Leftrightarrow \mathrm{form}\ 43. \tag{$\ast $} \end{equation*}$$

Also in Brunner [1983b] (p 437 Satz 2.2 (1)) is the result

$$\begin{equation*} \mathrm{form}\ [106 A]\Rightarrow \mathrm{form}\ 106 \tag{$\ast \ast $} \end{equation*}$$

In the $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ model $\mathcal{N}2$, form [106 A] is true and form 43 is false. Thus, combining $(\ast )$ and $(\ast \ast )$, we get the result that form 154 is not a theorem of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$.

NOTE 99

Form 65 (Krein-Milman Theorem) does not imply form 14 (BPI) in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. The argument is as follows: By results of Bell/Jellett [1971], form 14 + form 65 implies form 1 (AC). By Pincus [1972] and [1972], 65 is true and 1 is false in $\mathcal{N}2$ hence form 14 is false in $\mathcal{N}2$. Similarly, form 52 does not imply form 286 in ZF since form 52 + form 286 implies form 1 (Bell/Jellett [1971]) and by Pincus [1972], form 52 does not imply form 14 in ZF.

NOTE 100

In this note we show that in $\mathcal{N}23\,C(\infty ,\,2)$ (form 88) is false and $C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )$ (form 126) is true. The proof that $C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )$ is true is due to A. Rubin.

First we shall show that $C(\infty ,\,2)$ is false. Let $B$ be the set of subsets $x$ of $A$ such that the order type of $x$ with respect to $<$ is $\omega$. Let $D$ be the set of equivalence classes of elements of $B$ under the relation $xRy$ iff the symmetric difference, $(x-y) \cup (y-x)$ is finite. (Denote the equivalence class of $x$ by $[x]$.) Let $P$ be the set of pairs of elements of $D$. $P$ has no choice function in the model because if $f$ is such a choice function and $E\subseteq A$ is a support of $f$ it follows that for all order preserving permutations $\phi$ of $A$ such that $\phi$ fixes $E$ pointwise and for all $[x],\, [y]$ in $D$, if $\phi$ fixes $\{[x],\,[y]\}$ then $\phi$ fixes both $[x]$ and $[y]$. We can construct a $\phi ,\,x$ and $y$ for which this is false as follows: Since $E$ is well ordered there are elements $a,\,b\in A$ such that the interval $(a,\,b)$ contains no points of $E$. Let $\phi$ be an order preserving permutation of $A$ that fixes $E$ pointwise, fixes $a$ and $b$ but moves at least one element $t$ of $(a,\,b)$. We may assume (by replacing $\phi$ with $\phi ^{-1}$ if necessary) that $t<\phi (t)$. Let $x=\{\phi ^{2n}(t):n\in \omega \}$ and $y=\{\phi ^{2n+1}(t):n\in \omega \}$. Then $\phi ([x])=[y]$ and $\phi ([y])=[x] ($and $[x]\neq [y])$.

Next, we shall show that $C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )$ is true in $\mathcal{N}23$. Let $X=\{Y_{i}:i\in \omega \}$ be a denumerable set of non-empty sets in the model. Let $B$ be a common support for $X$ and the $Y_{i}$’s, $i\in \omega$. Let the open intervals of $A-B$ be denoted by $I_{\beta }$, for $\beta <\alpha$. For each $i\in \omega$, choose (in the outer model) $z_{i}\in Y_{i}$ and let $B_{i}$ be a support of $z_{i}$. Let $J_{\beta i}=I_{\beta }\cap B_{i}$. (Note: Whenever we choose a sequence of elements in $A$, we choose them in increasing order. Also, $\beta$ will range over $\alpha$, and $i$ and $j$ will range over $\omega$.)

We then define $K_{\beta ji}$ as follows: For each $\beta$ and $i$, choose $E_{\beta i}=\{e_{\beta ji}:j\in \omega \}$ cofinal in $I_{\beta }$ such that each $e_{\beta oi}<J_{\beta i}$ and $E_{\beta i}\cap \mathrm{cl}(B_{i})=\emptyset$. Then define $K_{\beta ji}= B_{i}\cap (e_{\beta ji},\,e_{\beta j+1i})$. (If $J_{\beta i}$ is not cofinal in $I_{\beta }$, choose $E_{\beta i}$ such that $e_{\beta oi}<J_{\beta i}<e_{\beta 1i}$ so there is only one non-empty $K_{\beta ji}$.)

For each $\beta$, choose $\{c_{\beta i}:i\in \omega \}$ cofinal in $I_{\beta }$ and choose $\{d_{\beta ji}:i\in \omega \}$ in the interval $(c_{\beta j},\,c_{\beta j+1})$. For each $\beta ,\,j$, and $i$, let $f_{\beta ji}$ be a function mapping $K_{\beta ji}$ into the interval $(d_{\beta ji},\,d_{\beta ji+1})$ and let $L_{\beta ji}$ be the range of $f_{\beta ji}$. Next, let $f_{i}$ be an extension of $\bigcup _{\beta ,j}f_{\beta ji}$ to a complete isomorphism of $A$ fixing $B$. We claim that $F=\{<Y_{i},\,f_{i}(z_{i})>:i\in \omega \}$ is a choice function for $X$ that is in the model. Since $f_{i}$ preserves $B$, we must have that $f_{i}(z_{i})\in f(Y_{i})=Y_{i}$. A support of $F$ is $\bigcup _{\beta ,j,i}L_{\beta ji}$ which is a well ordered union of the well ordered sets $L_{\beta ji}$ and, therefore, can be well ordered.

NOTE 101

The argument that form 43 (DC) implies [43 S] (If $S$ is a relation on $A$ such that $(\forall x\in A)(\exists y\in A)(x\,S\,y)$ and $x_{0}$ is any element of A, then there is a sequence $a(1),a(2),\ldots$ of elements of $A$ such that $a(n)\,S\,a(n+1)$ for all $n\in \omega$ and such that $a(0)=x_{0}.)$ is as follows: Let $S$ be a relation on a set $A$ satisfying the hypotheses of [43 S] and assume that $x_{0}\in A$. Let $B$ be the set of finite sequences $y=\langle y(i)\rangle _{i=0}^{n}$ of distinct elements of $A$ such that $y(0)=x_{0}$ and $y(i)\,S\,y(i+1)$ for $i=0$ to $n-1$. Define $R$ on $B$ by $y\,R\,z\Leftrightarrow y$ is a proper initial segment of $z$. Then the relation $R$ on $B$ satisfies the hypotheses of form 43. The conclusion of form 43 gives a sequence $y_{0}\,R\,y_{1}\,R\,y_{2}\,\ldots$ which gives an infinite sequence of elements of $A$ satisfying the conclusion of [43 S].
